newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICA SEES FIGHTING CHANCE TO HOST OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICA SEES FIGHTING CHANCE TO HOST OLYMPICS.

text.p: South Africa will step up its campaign over the next month to underpin "a fighting chance" of hosting the Olympic Games in 2004, Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said on Thursday.
"We started off with the perspective that we didn't have much of a chance, but in the past few months the pace has hotted up in our favour," he said in an interview.
"There is a feeling now that we can make a strong bid, that we have a fighting chance."
South Africa is widely regarded as an outsider in the five-city contest, but local campaigners believe the "Mandela factor" could swing the decision in favour of Cape Town on September 5.
Rome is favoured to win the contest from Athens, Stockholm, Buenos Aires and Cape Town.

President Nelson Mandela has strongly endorsed Cape Town's bid, saying repeatedly that the Olympic Movement owes it to Africa, represented by the fifth ring of the Olympic symbol, to stage the games on the continent for the first time.
"The president is very, very optimistic. He believes that we have earned the right to stage the Games in 2004," his spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters.
Pahad said Mandela and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki would concentrate over the next few weeks on initiatives to bolster Cape Town's bid.
"Our initial planning was not based on very great experience on how to bid for something like this and the government maybe came in a bit late.

"It is important for us to use the president and the deputy president a little more aggressively in this last phase. We must increase our contact with the IOC (International Olympic Committee) and other governments," he said.
Mankahlana said Mandela had plans to promote the bid, but declined to give details.
"The president is paying due attention to the mobilisation of the IOC and the international community to take a decision in favour of South Africa," he said.
Pahad said South Africa was honing its tactics as it became clear strategy, not just the detailed plan for the games, played an important part in winning the right to host the Olympics.
"Hopefully, we have got the African vote. If Argentina drops out in the first round of voting it is possible that we could attract some of the Latin American votes," he said.
IOC delegates will vote in secret, eliminating stragglers until a clear winner city emerges.
The divided European vote also could help, Pahad said.
"There is no collective European vote and we haven't seen any sign that they have already tactically agreed that if one drops out they will support the others."
"We strongly believe it is the time for Africa. There is so much going for us now in the sense of the period we're in, the Mandela factor and our transition," he said.
Mankahlana said Mandela would be in Lausanne, Switzerland, for the announcement of the winner next month.
